{{Short description|Astronomer}}

'''Ian Stewart Glass''' (born 5 September 1939 in Dublin, Ireland) is an infrared astronomer and scientific historian living in Cape Town, South Africa.

== Education ==

Glass was educated at Trinity College Dublin where he was a Foundation Scholar.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.tcdlife.ie/scholars/scholar/about-list.php |title=List of scholars - Scholars - TCD |publisher=Tcdlife.ie |date=2016-10-31 |accessdate=2022-03-15}}</ref> He obtained his B.A. with first class honours in 1961 and was awarded the Hackett Prize for first place in Natural Sciences. He received his PhD in Physics<ref>{{cite web|url=http://library.mit.edu/item/000599351|title=PDS SSO|website=library.mit.edu|access-date=2017-10-27}}</ref> from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1968 for work in x-ray astronomy under [[George W. Clark]].

== Infrared astronomy ==

Since 1970 he has worked in [[infrared astronomy]] and instrumentation<ref name="gm"/> and he has written the standard textbook on the subject.<ref name="handbook">{{cite book|last=Glass|first=I.S.|title=Handbook of Infrared Astronomy|date=1999|isbn=0-521-63311-7|publisher=Cambridge University press}}</ref>
He worked before 1975 at the [[Royal Greenwich Observatory]] and thereafter at the [[South African Astronomical Observatory]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.saao.ac.za/science/staff-research/ian-glass |title=Ian Glass: SAAO |access-date=27 March 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130519050105/http://www.saao.ac.za/science/staff-research/ian-glass/ |archive-date=19 May 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He is the author or co-author of over 220 scientific papers in journals and conference proceedings and has been cited over 11000 times with h-index=60.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.co.za/citations?user=fZ4uI20AAAAJ&hl=en|title=Ian S Glass}}</ref> <ref>scholar.google.com/scholar?="Ian+Glass"</ref>

With [[Tom Lloyd-Evans]], he discovered the [[period–luminosity relation]] followed by Mira variable stars.<ref name=plrel>{{cite journal|last1=Glass|first1=I.S.|last2=Lloyd Evans|first2=T.|year=1981|title=A period–luminosity relation for Mira variables in the Large Magellanic Cloud|journal=Nature| publisher=Macmillan|volume=291|issue=5813|pages=303–4|bibcode = 1981Natur.291..303G |doi = 10.1038/291303a0 |s2cid=4262929}}</ref> This result has subsequently been refined.<ref name=plrel2>{{cite conference|last1=Glass|first1=I.S.|last2=Catchpole|first2=R.M.| last3=Feast|first3=M.W.|last4=Whitelock|first4=P.A.|last5=Reid|first5=I.N.| title=The period–luminosity relationship for Mira-like variables in the LMC| conference=Late stages of stellar evolution, Calgary, Canada, 2–5 June 1986| editor1-last=Kwok|editor1-first=S.|editor2-last=Pottasch|editor2-first=S.R.| year=1987|pages=51–4|publisher=D. Reidel Publishing Co.| location=Dordrecht, Netherlands}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Feast|first1=M.W.|last2=Glass|first2=I.S.| last3=Whitelock|first3=P.A.|last4=Catchpole|first4=R.M.|date=1989|title=A period-luminosity-colour relation for Mira variables|journal=[[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]]|volume=241|issue=3|pages=375–92|doi=10.1093/mnras/241.3.375 |bibcode = 1989MNRAS.241..375F |doi-access=free}}</ref> Later observations of the Miras in the SgrI Baade's Window field led to an independent estimate of the distance to the Galactic Centre.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Glass|
first1=I.S.|last2=Whitelock|first2=P.A.|last3=Catchpole|first3=R.M.| last4=Feast|first4=M.W.| date=1995|title=Long-period variables in the SGR I field of the Galactic Bulge|journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|volume=273|
issue=2|pages=383–400|doi=10.1093/mnras/273.2.383 |bibcode = 1995MNRAS.273..383G |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 1973 Feast and Glass<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Glass|first1=I.S.| last2=Feast|first2=M.W.|title=Peculiar object near GX2+5| journal=Nature Physical Science|date=1973|volume=245|issue=142|pages=39–40|bibcode = 1973NPhS..245...39G |doi = 10.1038/physci245039b0 }}</ref> discovered the infrared/optical counterpart of the symbiotic binary x-ray source GX1+4. In 1978 Glass located the obscured x-ray source [[Circinus X-1|Cir X-1]] in the infrared and found that it flared in a cyclic manner associated with its 16.6-day x-ray period.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Glass|first=I.S.|date=1978|title=Variations of Circinus X-1 in the infrared|journal= Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|volume=183|issue=3|pages=335–340|doi=10.1093/mnras/183.3.335 |bibcode=1978MNRAS.183..335G|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The role of hot dust in the emission from a [[Seyfert galaxy]] (Fairall 9) was demonstrated observationally for the first time by Clavel, Wamsteker and Glass in 1989;<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Clavel|first1=J.|last2=Wamsteker| first2=W.|last3=Glass |first3=I.S.|date=1989|title=Hot dust on the outskirts of the broad-line region in Fairall 9 |journal=Astrophysical Journal|publisher=[[University of Chicago Press]]|volume=337| pages=236–250|doi=10.1086/167100|bibcode=1989ApJ...337..236C}}</ref> 
<ref>{{cite journal|last=Shields|first=G.A.|year=1999|title=A brief history of AGN|journal=Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific|volume=111|pages=661-678}}</ref>
These observations were modelled theoretically by Barvainis<ref>{{cite journal|last=Barvainis |first=R.|date=1992|title=Dust reverberations: a model for the infrared variations of Fairall 9|journal=Astrophysical Journal|publisher=University of Chicago Press|volume=400|pages=502–509|bibcode = 1992ApJ...400..502B |doi = 10.1086/172012 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and provided a strong confirmation of the reverberation model<ref>{{cite journal|last=Peterson|first=B.M.| title=Reverberation mapping of active galactic nuclei| journal=Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific|date=1993|volume=105| pages=247–268|bibcode = 1993PASP..105..247P |doi = 10.1086/133140 |arxiv=astro-ph/9706039|s2cid=123216750 }}</ref> for active galactic nuclei. The photometry was part of a multi-year monitoring programme<ref>{{cite journal|last=Glass|first=I.S.| year=2004|title=Long-term infrared photometry of Seyferts|journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|volume=350|issue=3| pages=1048–1066|doi=10.1111/j.1365-2966.2004.07712.x|doi-access=free | bibcode=2004MNRAS.350.1049G|arxiv = astro-ph/0402289 |s2cid=15194743}}</ref> that showed the ubiquity of infrared variability in these objects.

Work with the ISO satellite and MACHO data showed that all late-type M giant stars exhibit mass-loss and are variable.<ref name=ringberg>{{cite conference|last1=Glass|first1=I.S.|last2=Alves|first2=D.R.|title=ISOGAL Survey of Baade's Windows
|conference=ISO Surveys of a Dusty Universe, Ringberg, 1999|editor1-last=Lemke|editor1-first=D. |editor2-last=Stickel |editor2-first=M.| editor3-last=Wilke |editor3-first=K.| date=2000| pages=363–70| publisher=Springer| location=Heidelberg|isbn=3-540-67479-9}}</ref>

The most detailed image of the Galactic Centre (inner Bulge) region before the advent of array detectors was obtained with Catchpole and Whitelock in 1987,<ref>{{cite journal| last1=Glass|
first1=I.S.|last2=Catchpole|first2=R.M.|last3=Whitelock|first3=P.A.|title=J, H and K maps of the Galactic centre region.II – Qualitative aspects of the interstellar absorption|journal=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|date=1987|volume=227|
issue=2|pages=373–79|bibcode = 1987MNRAS.227..373G | doi = 10.1093/mnras/227.2.373 |doi-access=free}}</ref> showing up extinction patterns that correlated with the intervening molecular clouds.

== History of astronomy ==

In addition to papers on a number of historical themes, Glass has written several books (see below):

"Victorian Telescope Makers" was inspired by the extensive correspondence between [[David Gill (astronomer)|Sir David Gill]] and the Irish telescope maker [[Howard Grubb|Sir Howard Grubb]] that survives at the South African Astronomical Observatory.

"Revolutionaries of the Cosmos" deals with eight figures (Galileo, Newton, Herschel, Huggins, Hale, Shapley, Eddington and Hubble) who revolutionised physical astronomy through the introduction of radical new ideas and techniques.

[[Nicolas Louis de Lacaille|"Nicolas-Louis de La Caille"]] concerns the leading observational astronomer of the mid-eighteenth century who was also the first important scientist to visit what is now South Africa (1751–53). Inter alia, he conducted the first telescope sky survey, was a devotee of Newtonian dynamics and a pioneer of the Lunar method of navigation.

"Grubb Dublin and Grubb Parsons" relates the history of the telescope company founded in Dublin ca 1830 and located in more recent years at Newcastle upon Tyne, before its closure in 1985.

== Honours, etc ==

Glass received the Gill Medal<ref name=gm>{{cite journal|last=Lloyd Evans|first=T.|date=1999|title=Gill Medal awarded to Ian Stewart Glass|journal=Monthly Notes of the Astronomical Society of Southern Africa|volume=58|pages=101–2|bibcode = 1999MNSSA..58..101. }}</ref> of the Astronomical Society of Southern Africa in 1999 for his work in the infrared and their McIntyre Award in 2003 for his book on the Grubb Telescope Company (see below).

He is a member of the [[Royal Society of South Africa]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.royalsocietysa.org.za/?page_id=136|title=Members|date=5 July 2012|publisher=|access-date=26 March 2013|archive-date=6 August 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120806225255/http://www.royalsocietysa.org.za/?page_id=136|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the [[International Astronomical Union]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iau.org/administration/membership/individual/1827/|title=International Astronomical Union - IAU|website=www.iau.org}}</ref>
He has twice been elected president of the [[Astronomical Society of Southern Africa]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://assa.saao.ac.za|title=ASSA|website=ASSA}}</ref> and in 2016 was made an honorary member thereof.

In 1984–89 he was editor of "Monthly Notes of the Astronomical Society of Southern Africa".

He has been a visiting professor at the [[National Astronomical Observatory of Japan]] (Nobeyama and Tokyo), an associate of the [[European Southern Observatory]] and has worked for various periods at the [[California Institute of Technology]], the [[University of Arizona]], the [[Institut d'astrophysique de Paris]] (France), the [[Observatoire de Besançon]], the [[Institute of Astronomy, Cambridge]] (UK) and the [[Physical Research Laboratory]], Ahmedabad (India). He has also been an adjunct professor at [[James Cook University]], Queensland, Australia.

* Glass, I.S. (2008) [https://web.archive.org/web/20170912173553/http://www.saao.ac.za/~isg/proxima.html Proxima: The Nearest Star (other than the Sun), Mons Mensa, Cape Town (self-published)], {{ISBN|978-0-9814126-0-3}}.
* Glass, I.S. (2013) Nicolas-Louis de La Caille – Astronomer and Geodesist, Oxford University Press, Oxford, {{ISBN|978-0-19-966840-3}}. French edition translated by James Lequeux, EDP Sciences ({{ISBN|978-2-7598-0999-8}}) and Observatoire de Paris ({{ISBN|978-2-901057-68-0}}.
* Glass, I.S. (2015) [http://www.saao.ac.za/~isg/royalobservatory.html The Royal Observatory at the Cape of Good Hope: History and Heritage, Mons Mensa, Cape Town (self-published).] Available as pdf, free, from CfAH.org.za/resources/rocgh-glass. {{ISBN|978-0-9814126-2-7}}.
* Glass, I.S. (2026) [http://www.saao.ac.za/~isg/grubbgp.html Grubb Dublin and Grubb Parsons, Mons Mensa, Cape Town (Self Published)]. Available as pdf, free, from CfAH.org.za/resources/grubb-glass.
